cues.text: MIT 8105, Network Architecture and Protocols.
This is Study Session 5, Software-Defined Networking, usually shortened to SDN.
We begin with chapter one, SDN foundations.
To understand SDN, we first need to understand how traditional networks are built.
In a traditional router or switch, two different jobs live inside the same device.
The first is the control plane.
The control plane decides forwarding paths: it works out where traffic should go.
The second is the data plane.
The data plane does the forwarding: it actually moves packets according to those decisions.
In traditional networks, both planes sit together in every device, and the devices often coordinate through distributed routing protocols.
Each router runs its own protocol software, talks to its neighbours, and builds its own picture of the network.
There is also a third idea, the management plane.
The management plane configures and observes devices.
It is how administrators set devices up, and how they watch what the devices are doing.
Software-defined networking changes this arrangement.
SDN separates control logic from forwarding, and it exposes programmable abstractions.
In other words, the decision-making is pulled out of each individual box, and it is offered to software through interfaces that programs can use.
One phrase needs care here: logically centralised control.
It means that the network has unified policy and a unified network view.
It does not necessarily mean a single physical controller.
Controllers can be run as a cluster, and a cluster can provide resilience.
So the control is one logical brain, even if several machines share the work.
Now let us look at the layered picture that accompanies this.
Please refer to the diagram on screen as I describe it from top to bottom.
At the top are the applications.
The examples shown are traffic engineering, security and automation.
These are programs that want the network to behave in certain ways.
Between the applications and the controller, there is a link labelled the northbound API.
The northbound API is how the applications talk down to the controller.
The next layer is the controller.
The diagram lists what it holds: topology, policy, path computation and state.
So the controller knows how the network is connected, what rules apply, how to compute paths, and what condition the network is currently in.
Below the controller there is a link labelled the southbound interface.
This is how the controller talks down to the devices.
The next layer holds the switches and routers.
The diagram lists their actions: match, forward, drop, modify and count.
So these devices examine traffic and match it against rules, and then they forward it, drop it, or modify it.
They also count it.
Below the switches and routers, the link is labelled data traffic, and at the very bottom are the endpoints.
The endpoints are the devices that send and receive the actual traffic.
The hierarchy therefore runs from applications, to controller, to switches and routers, to endpoints.
Control and policy come down from above, and data traffic flows between the devices and the endpoints.
Let us now name these interfaces more precisely.
Northbound APIs expose network abstractions to applications.
They are often REST or gRPC interfaces, or model-driven interfaces.
The southbound side communicates with devices, using protocols such as OpenFlow, NETCONF with YANG, and P4Runtime, along with other approaches.
Beyond north and south, there is also east-west communication.
East-west communication coordinates controllers or domains with one another.
A very important warning follows.
SDN is not synonymous with OpenFlow.
OpenFlow is one southbound option, not the definition of SDN.
Some systems retain distributed protocols under central orchestration.
So an SDN design might still let routers run their usual protocols, while a central system directs and coordinates them.
Remember too the management plane.
It handles configuration, telemetry and administration.
Finally, let us weigh up the benefits and the challenges.
The benefits are rapid provisioning, consistent policies, automation, traffic engineering, visibility, virtual networks, and reduced manual device-by-device change.
Instead of logging in to many devices one at a time, you express the change once and apply it consistently.
The challenges are these: controller availability and security, scale, latency, interoperability, legacy integration, skills, state consistency, and troubleshooting.
One further point deserves emphasis.
Centralised control can increase the blast radius of mistakes.
A single wrong policy, pushed from the centre, can reach many devices at once.

So the source recommends these protective practices: use authenticated management, use RBAC, which stands for role-based access control, use controller redundancy, use tested policies, and have safe rollback.
Together, these let you gain the power of central control while limiting the damage if something goes wrong.
